ratings.note: Web PWA on any Chromium OS (Win/Mac/Linux/ChromeOS) plus a Windows Electron .exe; no tablet/mobile UI; packaged .exe never built or run.
Windows and macOS desktop; Linux frozen at legacy 1.7; no web or tablet. Solid dual-desktop, narrower than the browser rivals.
Windows and macOS desktop only; no Linux, no web/mobile. Same dual-desktop reach as sibling LightBurn but no legacy Linux build.
Windows-only (.NET/WinForms); Mac and Linux need Wine or a VM. Narrowest OS coverage in the roster.
xTool Studio on Windows/macOS desktop plus iOS/Android/iPad apps with cloud sync; strong cross-device but no Linux and no web.
Browser-based on Windows/macOS/Linux/Chromebook via multiple browsers; broadest OS reach in the roster, tablet included; web-only, no native.
Native Windows/macOS/Linux plus Raspberry Pi; broadest native-desktop coverage in the roster, but no web or mobile client.
Fully-offline installable PWA with mid-burn-safe updates; desktop auto-update ships unsigned with no signature check, and offline/update never verified on a device.
Installed desktop app, fully offline (periodic online license recheck); manual Check-for-Updates gated to the license's valid update window.
Installed desktop app, offline-capable; current/previous/beta builds with a manual updater. Same install/update model as sibling LightBurn.
Lightweight free Windows installer, fully offline once installed; GitHub-release notifications, but dormant with no release in ~16 months.
In-app auto-update, but login/cloud drives material library and sync so some features need connectivity; XCS itself is EOL.
No install, always latest, zero update friction; but internet required to load/save, and offline edits cannot be saved until reconnected.
Free installer for all four platforms, fully offline, in-app update guide and frequent releases; smoothest, friction-free install/update story in the roster.
Refuse-before-freeze budgets plus Web Workers and decimated strokes, but entirely unmeasured; known O(N^2) streamer, App-root re-render storm, uncached raster compile remain.
Native C++/Qt handles large work but community reports lag as objects/nodes and heavy traces pile up; a restart restores speed.
Inferred parity with LightBurn's native engine; too young for an independent community performance record. Parity assumed, not confirmed.
Lightweight native, fast on large raster-to-G-code even on modest hardware, but community notes certain JPEGs crash it.
Weakest here: docs admit lag and white-screen crashes on complex images even at recommended specs; mitigations compress images and disable precise vector paths.
Browser-bounded: large or many-path SVG imports bog down the canvas; community guidance is to simplify paths before import.
Electron sender loads and visualizes large G-code; 3D visualizer can lag on some GPUs; startup was cut from ~25s to ~4s.
ErrorBoundary crash screen, 30s autosave, boot restore, fingerprint checkpoint resume; two known bugs (phantom restore prompt, selective-job resume dead-end); checkpoint HW-CLAIMED.
Configurable auto-save plus a post-crash reload prompt from Documents; community reports it occasionally saves empty or loses recovery on a double-crash.
Inferred parity (same engine); a patch hardened malformed-file loading to report errors, and it keeps the last 50 preference backups.
Stable in normal use but no project auto-save or crash recovery, and certain files crash it; recovery means re-importing the source.
Cloud project storage makes work recoverable across devices, but blank-screen/freeze crashes on import are documented; no local auto-save prompt.
Strongest recovery: continuous server-side saving reopens the project after a browser/tab crash with little loss; offline edits lost if closed before reconnecting.
As a sender there is no design to lose; generally stable, persists settings, offers a diagnostic file; job-level recovery sits under execution.
Tested, DoS-capped, Result-typed .lf2 save degrades not crashes, but schema frozen at v1 with empty migrators; downgrade silently drops unknown blocks.
Mature XML .lbrn2/.lbrn; lossless both directions, smaller/faster since 2.0, long track record of opening old files. Robust, near-human-readable.
Binary .mage (art, toolpaths, tools, material, layout); cross-compatible with LightBurn; a patch improved damaged-file handling. Young but solid.
No design project format: operates on imported images and G-code only, so there is nothing versioned to save or migrate.
Native .xcs with cloud storage and cross-device sharing, tied to xTool accounts; robustness adequate, migration path points toward xTool Studio.
Projects live server-side, so versioning/migration is vendor-managed and users never hit format breakage; downside is no offline file or exposed version history.
No design project format; closest analog is robust versioned settings and firmware/EEPROM backup-restore via the Config tab. No project-migration concept.
Disciplined caps (undo, transcripts, WeakMap) but a known unbounded raster-cache leak (~800MB worst case) plus Electron/browser heft; footprint never measured.
Native C++/Qt with a modest footprint versus Electron/browser rivals; 4GB minimum, 16GB for heavy images. Efficient for its capability.
Inferred from the shared codebase: same native engine and specs as LightBurn (8GB recommended, ~450MB install); comparable footprint, not independently benchmarked.
Lightest in the roster: a small native .NET app that runs happily on old, low-spec PCs. Featherweight is its whole appeal.
Heaviest desktop footprint: needs 8GB+ RAM and a capable GPU; docs recommend closing other apps and staying plugged in to avoid lag.
Footprint is a browser tab, bounded by the browser and partly server-offloaded; heavy designs still tax browser RAM. 64-bit only.
Electron but deliberately lean: 2GB minimum, targets Raspberry Pi and mini-PCs; heavier than a bare native sender but single-board-capable.

wins.claim: KerfDesk ships an ErrorBoundary crash screen, 30s autosave, a boot restore prompt and a fingerprint-gated checkpoint resume, where LaserGRBL has no project auto-save or crash recovery at all.
A fully-offline installable PWA with mid-burn-safe updates versus XCS's cloud-tethered, now-EOL update path that expects connectivity for its material library and sync.
The web PWA runs on macOS, Linux and ChromeOS via any Chromium browser, reaching platforms MillMage's Windows-and-macOS-only desktop cannot.

gaps.claim: Resource footprint: an Electron/browser stack plus a known unbounded raster-preview cache leak (~800MB static worst case) versus LaserGRBL's featherweight native app; footprint never measured.
Large-design performance is entirely unmeasured (static call-path analysis only) with a known O(N^2) streamer, App-root re-render storm and uncached raster compile still unfixed.
Project format frozen at schema v1 with an empty migrator registry, so an older build silently drops unknown blocks on downgrade, and no historical .lf2 corpus loads in CI.
Crash recovery is local-only with two confirmed seam bugs (phantom restore prompt, selective-job resume dead-end) versus Easel's continuous server-side save.
Desktop auto-update ships unsigned with no code-signature verification (a security-adjacent tamper window), and offline install/update was never verified on a device.
No tablet/mobile UI and the packaged Windows .exe is never built or run in CI, so platform drift between release tags goes uncaught.

notVerified: 17.1 — no packaged Windows .exe was built, opened or run by anyone (release-manual); no macOS/Linux, tablet or touch UI verified to exist; WebSerial availability on mobile/tablet Chromium unconfirmed; CI exercises only the ubuntu web target, so Windows platform drift between release tags is uncaught.

17.2 — packaged-Electron install-on-quit update, and whether Chromium actually refuses SW registration on the app:// scheme, were never run (inferred from config/code); the unsigned-update tamper window is proven from config only, not exploited; real offline install/update on a device not exercised.

17.3 — no runtime profiling of any kind (read-only, no dev server, no hardware): all frame-rate, compile-duration and memory-growth claims are static call-path analysis; production-scale big-SVG/big-raster/many-object behavior not measured; the 120k-segment decimated-display perceptual quality not checked.

17.4 — hardware crash+resume is HW-CLAIMED (ADR-118); real force-kill and localStorage quota-exhaustion autosave behavior not exercised; Electron-side localStorage persistence config not read (renderer path only); the phantom-restore and selective-resume verdicts are static, not reproduced in a running app this pass.

17.5 — no committed corpus of real historical .lf2 files (one per shipped phase) is loaded in CI, so 'every version loads' rests on synthetic per-feature fixtures; downgrade data-loss is inferred from current normalizers, not run against an actual older build; whether GRBL rejects the +Infinity-derived line was not tested.

17.6 — no memory or CPU measurement at typical or heavy load by anyone (read-only, no dev server, no hardware); the ~800MB raster-cache figure and the capped-undo-stack footprint are static worst-case estimates, not observed.

Both sides are documentary or code, never hardware or benchmarked — every competitor performance/footprint cell is [OFF]/[COMM]/[INF], none [HANDS]; the [INF] cells (MillMage 17.3, 17.4, 17.6) are not load-bearing and no win/lose bullet rests on them.
U cells: none in this sector — all 42 cells (6 categories x 7 products) carry code or documentary evidence.
